## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 3/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
State of the art (as of July 2026) in AI coding-agent governance and harness design — the problem space of the claude.md-workflow repo: project instruction files (CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md-style), lifecycle hooks, deterministic verification gates, persistent agent memory/working-state across sessions and compaction, behavioral guardrails against scope creep/overclaiming/sycophancy, git-level enforcement, task contracts, and parallel multi-agent orchestration (worktree isolation, orchestrator/reduce patterns, adversarial review). Survey and compare best practices from: Anthropic (Claude Code, Agent SDK, skills/hooks/subagents), OpenAI (Codex, AGENTS.md), Google (Gemini CLI/Jules/Antigravity), Microsoft (GitHub Copilot agents, AutoGen/agent frameworks), NVIDIA (agent toolkits/NeMo), xAI (Grok agents/coding); and non-Western labs: Moonshot AI (Kimi K2.5 agentic training), Zhipu/Z.ai (GLM-5.x coding agents), DeepSeek (agentic/tool-use practices), Tencent (recent Hunyuan model launch and agent tooling), MiniMax (M-series agentic models), Alibaba Qwen if relevant; plus respected independents: Nous Research (Hermes 4/Hermes agent), Fundamental Research Labs (Peter Wang co-founder), the team behind the Ornith-1.0 LLM, tinygrad/George Hotz's approach to minimal harnesses, and any other influential open agent-harness projects (e.g. OpenHands, SWE-agent, Aider, Cline, Devin/Cognition). For each: what they prescribe for instruction-file structure and length, memory persistence, verification/eval gating, multi-agent patterns, and prompt-vs-deterministic enforcement. Identify convergent consensus, notable divergences (especially Western vs Chinese lab practices), and concrete, citable insights that should shape a 2026 rewrite of a drop-in governance kit for coding agents. Note if any named entity cannot be verified to exist (e.g. 'Ornith-1.0') rather than guessing.

## Claim under review
"An adversarial, stage-gated multi-agent review pipeline (Refute-or-Promote) killed roughly 79% of ~171 defect candidates before disclosure over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets, with an 83% prospective kill rate on a consolidated-protocol subset (n=30), demonstrating that most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives that structured adversarial gating can filter out."

**Source:** https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049 (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "Over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets (security libraries, the ISO C++ standard, major compilers), the pipeline killed ∼79% of ∼171 candidates before advancing to disclosure (retrospective aggregate); on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n = 30), the prospective kill rate was 83%."

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

# Paper Summary

**Title:** Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery

**Author:** Abhinav Agarwal

**Does it match your description?** Yes, precisely.

**Relevant Abstract Quote:**
"Over a 31-day campaign across 7 targets... the pipeline killed roughly 79% of 171 candidates before advancing to disclosure; on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n=30), the prospective kill rate was 83%."

The paper describes exactly the methodology you outlined—an adversarial multi-agent review system that systematically filters false positive defect candidates through staged gates, achieving the specific kill rates and metrics you referenced.

Web search results for query: ""Refute-or-Promote" adversarial pipeline defect candidates "kill rate" wolfSSL lcms2"

Links: [{"title":"Refute-or-Promote: Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery","url":"https://arxiv.org/html/2604.19049"},{"title":"[2604.19049] Refute-or-Promote: An Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review Methodology for High-Precision LLM-Assisted Defect Discovery","url":"https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.19049"},{"title":"Refute-or-Promote: Adversarial Stage-Gated Multi-Agent Review","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.19049"},{"title":"Software Engineering","url":"https://arxiv.org/list/cs.SE/new"},{"title":"Refute-or-Promote: Adversarial Multi-Agent Review for High-Precision Defect Discovery - YouTube","url":"https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P97IaH-98L0"},{"title":"OpenAnt: LLM-Powered Vulnerability Discovery Through Code Decomposition, Adversarial Verification, and Dynamic Testing","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.19149"},{"title":"Adversarial Bug Reports as a Security Risk in Language Model-Based Automated Program Repair","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.05372"},{"title":"Iterative Audit Convergence in LLM-Managed Multi-Agent Systems: A Case Study in Prompt-Engineering Quality Assurance","url":"https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.12280"}]

Based on the search results, here's what I found:

Refute-or-Promote is an inference-time reliability pattern combining Stratified Context Hunting (SCH) for candidate generation, adversarial kill mandates, context asymmetry, and a Cross-Model Critic (CMC). Adversarial agents attempt to disprove candidates at each promotion gate; cold-start reviewers are intended to reduce anchoring cascades; cross-family review can catch correlated blind spots that same-family review misses.

Regarding the kill rate for the defect candidates in wolfSSL and lcms2 specifically: on a consolidated-protocol subset (lcms2, wolfSSL; n=30), the prospective kill rate was 83%. This contrasts with the pipeline killed roughly 79% of 171 candidates before advancing to disclosure (retrospective aggregate) across all seven targets tested.

Refute-or-Promote is presented in its final standardised form as a four-stage adversarial protocol, with later campaigns (lcms2, wolfSSL) applying the consolidated protocol more uniformly.

The paper is published on arXiv (2604.19049) and was published on April 21, 2026.

content.text: The paper exists and the quote matches. Let me check the paper's own limitations and whether killed candidates were verified as false positives, and whether it's peer-reviewed.

input.prompt: Answer these questions with quotes: (1) Were the ~79% "killed" candidates verified to be actual false positives, or just failed to survive review gates? Does the paper acknowledge killed candidates might have been real bugs (false negatives)? (2) What limitations does the paper state (single author, self-reported, no ground truth, retrospective reconstruction)? (3) What happened to the candidates that survived — were any confirmed as real bugs/CVEs by maintainers? (4) Is this peer-reviewed or a preprint? What venue?

content.content:
# Analysis of Refute-or-Promote Paper

## (1) False Positive vs. False Negative Verification

The paper **does not verify** that killed candidates were actual false positives. The author explicitly acknowledges this limitation:

> "False negatives and the unidirectional pipeline. Refute-or-Promote optimises precision but does not measure recall."

The paper further states: "One documented case confirms the false-negative risk...the lcms2 CubeSize() overflow (CVE-2026-41254) was unanimously killed and recovered only via human override."

This shows killed candidates could harbor real bugs that the pipeline incorrectly rejected.

## (2) Stated Limitations

The author lists several critical constraints:

> "Single operator with domain expertise (not independently replicated). No ablation studies isolating individual mechanisms."

Additionally: "Because the four-stage protocol evolved during the campaign, early successes...cannot be attributed solely to the final formulation; target selection, operator learning, and manual prompt iteration are confounders."

The paper acknowledges the ~79% kill rate is "a retrospective aggregate" rather than prospective measurement on a fixed protocol.

## (3) Survivors Confirmed as Real Bugs

Yes. The 36+ outcomes include:

> "4 CVEs [3 public, 1 embargoed]; LWG 4549 accepted to the ISO C++ Working Paper; 5 merged ISO C++ editorial PRs; 3 compiler conformance bugs; 8 merged security-related fixes without CVE"

These were externally validated through maintainer acceptance and CVE assignment.

## (4) Publication Status

This is a **preprint** (arXiv:2604.19049v1, dated April 2026). No peer-review status is indicated on the document itself.

input.evidence: The numeric portion is real and current: arXiv:2604.19049 ("Refute-or-Promote," Abhinav Agarwal, April 2026) exists and its abstract states verbatim that ~79% of ~171 candidates were killed over the 31-day, 7-target campaign, with an 83% prospective kill rate on the lcms2/wolfSSL n=30 subset. However, the claim's concluding clause — that this "demonstrat[es] that most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives that structured adversarial gating can filter out" — overreaches the source in ways the paper itself explicitly disclaims: (1) killed candidates were never verified to be false positives; the paper states the pipeline "optimises precision but does not measure recall," and documents at least one killed candidate that was a REAL bug (the lcms2 CubeSize() overflow, CVE-2026-41254, "unanimously killed and recovered only via human override"), so kill rate cannot be equated with false-positive rate; (2) the 79% figure is a "retrospective aggregate" over an evolving protocol with stated confounders ("target selection, operator learning, and manual prompt iteration are confounders"; "not independently replicated," "no ablation studies"); (3) this is a single-author, non-peer-reviewed preprint reporting a self-run campaign — insufficient source strength for the generalized claim that "most LLM-generated defect findings are false positives." The claim would survive only if trimmed to the raw kill-rate statistics with the causal/generalizing conclusion removed or heavily qualified.
